children: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) raised its key short-term interest rate by 25 basis points to 1.25% during its September meeting, matching market expectations and marking the highest policy rate in the country since April 1995.

The decision, approved in a 7-2 vote, represents the BOJ's first rate increase in three months as policymakers continue to dismantle decades of ultra-loose monetary policy. Board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato cast the dissenting votes.
Policymakers cited persistent inflation fueled by rising oil prices and corporate price pass-throughs, as the primary driver for the hike.
Core CPI inflation has been rising moderately as higher business-to-business prices spill over into consumer prices and firms pass higher wages on to selling prices.
The central bank highlighted upside risks that inflation could exceed its 2% target, noting that it will closely monitor ongoing geopolitical developments, including conflicts in the Middle East.

Looking ahead, BOJ officials signaled that further rate hikes remain on the table. The board stated it will continue adjusting monetary accommodation in line with economic activity, price trends, and financial conditions, while carefully weighing the timing and cadence of future adjustments.
